extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of social psychology / sociology (crowd psychology, public opinion, political sociology)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts conceptual criteria and characteristics describing how prestige, beliefs, and opinions operate in crowds — their types, sources, effects, durability, and how modern media and politics interact with them. Useful for interpreting mass persuasion and public opinion dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of prestige
rubrics_metrics.description: Prestige is a sort of domination exercised on our mind by an individual, a work, or an idea that paralyzes critical faculty and fills the soul with astonishment and respect; it is the mainspring of all authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prestige functions psychologically to block critical examination — treat any claim with high prestige as potentially immune to scrutiny. Examples: gods, kings, celebrated historical figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two principal kinds of prestige (acquired vs personal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prestige may be grouped into acquired (resulting from name, fortune, reputation, position, titles, uniforms) and personal (an individual, magnetic quality independent of rank or possessions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing influence, distinguish whether authority comes from external trappings (uniforms, titles, wealth) or from an intrinsic personal charisma that compels acceptance of ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquired (artificial) prestige — sources and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Acquired prestige arises from occupying a position, bearing titles, fortune, clothing/uniforms; it can confer authority regardless of personal worth (e.g., soldiers in uniform, judges in robes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to symbolic devices (robes, decorations, titles) that lend credibility. Pascal’s observation on wigs/robes: removal diminishes perceived authority. Examples and anecdotes illustrate social contagion of respect for status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prestige of works and ideas through repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary and artistic prestige often results from accumulated repetitions: historical repetition of judgments leads to unexamined reverence (e.g., Homer, the Parthenon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prestige in cultural artifacts is frequently self-reinforcing; popular consensus and educational transmission can make works immune to critique. Watch for ‘received opinion’ untested by readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal prestige (charismatic/magnetic authority)
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal prestige is an individual faculty that generates a magnetic fascination, forcing acceptance of ideas and obedience independent of institutional authority (examples: Buddha, Jesus, Mahomet, Joan of Arc, Napoleon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify leaders whose influence predates institutional power; their immediate personal impact (first impressions, comportment) can override rational opposition and mobilize followers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prestige grows with success and is vulnerable to failure
rubrics_metrics.description: Success is a principal stepping-stone to prestige; disappearance of success usually leads to rapid loss of prestige. The fallen hero is quickly reviled by the same crowd that once acclaimed him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate durability of prestige against the subject’s recent successes or failures; prestige derived chiefly from success is brittle and contingent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prestige is destroyed by discussion and proximity
rubrics_metrics.description: Prestige is worn away slowly by exposure to discussion and quickly when its objects are brought within easy critical reach; for the crowd to admire, it must be kept at a distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical scrutiny and open debate are reliable means to erode unjustified prestige. Intimacy/proximity reduces awe and increases equality, weakening prestige.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contagion and unconscious imitation driven by prestige
rubrics_metrics.description: Prestige produces imitation by contagion: individuals, artists, and entire generations unconsciously copy those endowed with prestige and believe in the sincerity of their imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When tracing cultural or stylistic trends, account for unconscious stylistic transmission from prestigious exemplars rather than deliberate, objective aesthetic choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed (general) beliefs — characteristics and societal role
rubrics_metrics.description: Great permanent beliefs endure for centuries, shape civilizations, are few in number, hard to uproot, and provide the framework and indispensable pillars of civilisation (examples: feudalism, Christianity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat foundational beliefs as powerful, slow-changing forces that determine institutions, arts, and customs. Attempts to change them tend to require revolutionary transformation and often meet intolerance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intolerance as a social virtue for preserving general beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: Nations instinctively display intolerance in defense of their core beliefs; such intolerance, though philosophically questionable, functions as a necessary social virtue to maintain cohesion and civilizational continuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand historical persecution or suppression of dissent as mechanisms for preserving foundational beliefs; this explains why innovators often meet harsh resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical absurdity does not prevent a belief's spread
rubrics_metrics.description: The evident philosophical absurdity of a general belief is no obstacle to its triumph; beliefs can hypnotize intelligence and be accepted even by great minds (e.g., religious legends accepted for centuries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reject the social power of a belief merely because it seems irrational; analyze its social functions and symbolic potency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanics of belief decline and institutional lag
rubrics_metrics.description: When a general belief is called into question it is doomed; however, associated institutions persist and decay slowly. Nations cannot change beliefs without transforming many elements of civilization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect long institutional inertia after ideological shifts; policy or cultural change must address entrenched institutional legacies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changeable opinions — nature and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Above fixed beliefs lie transient, surface opinions that arise and vanish quickly (literary/art movements, fashions); they are superficial, formed by suggestion and contagion, and not anchored to the race’s general beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between deep-seated beliefs and ephemeral opinions when predicting persistence of attitudes or trends; ephemeral opinions are susceptible to fleeting stimuli and competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons for increased volatility of opinions in modern times
rubrics_metrics.description: Three causes: weakening of old general beliefs freeing space for ephemeral opinions; growing power of crowds permitting mobility of ideas; and the newspaper press constantly exposing crowds to opposing opinions so no single opinion becomes stable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In modern mass societies expect greater opinion churn. Media saturation and crowd dynamics produce rapid, ephemeral shifts rather than entrenched consensus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Powerlessness of governments and media to direct opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: In the present age governments and writers no longer direct opinion; writers have lost influence and newspapers mainly reflect opinion; statesmen follow opinion and fear it, adopting unstable lines of conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy-makers should monitor opinion rather than assume they can easily shape it. The press tends to follow consumer demand (news/amusement), limiting its capacity to form long-term doctrinal positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changing role and limits of critics and the press
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics and newspapers can harm but not guarantee success; press has become an information/amusement industry, often reducing criticism to short 'puffs' rather than substantive review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not overestimate the gatekeeping power of critics or legacy papers in determining cultural success; for modern promotion, rely less on traditional critical endorsement and more on broader crowd dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowd indifference and political consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Destruction of general beliefs and lack of centralized direction of opinion lead to extreme divergence of convictions and growing crowd indifference to issues not touching immediate interests; politics increasingly swayed by sentiment rather than reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate populist or sentiment-driven political movements; issues not directly affecting material interests will tend to attract less sustained public engagement.
